findings.title: SHA-256 padded length is compared without range-checking the field element
findings.evidence: In Sha256General, line 126 wires the untrusted input `paddedInLength` directly into `bitLengthVerifier.in[0]` of `LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits)` (line 125) as the sole bound on the message length (expected `paddedInLength <= maxBitLength`). `paddedInLength` is a free field-element signal: the only other constraint on it is `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (line 111), where `inBlockIndex` is itself an unconstrained witness (`<--` at line 110). It is never range-checked to `maxBitsPaddedBits` bits. circomlib's `LessThan`/`LessEqThan` do not range-check their operands; they constrain `Num2Bits(n+1)` of `in[0] + 2^n - in[1] - 1` and test the MSB, so the comparison is performed modulo the BN254 prime. Because `paddedInLength` is unconstrained, a malicious prover can supply a value near the field modulus (e.g. `paddedInLength = p - 512*d` for small `d`) so that `2^n - maxBitLength - 1 - 512*d` is non-negative and the wrapped expression is < 2^n, making `bitLengthVerifier.out === 1` (line 128) satisfiable while `paddedInLength > maxBitLength`. The very same missing range check applies to `inBlockIndex` at the `ItemAtIndex` selection (line 195: `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1`), which is derived from the unvalidated `paddedInLength` and drives which SHA256 compression block output is selected. Thus the intended length bound is not enforced and the block index used to select the hash output is attacker-controlled, breaking the length binding of the SHA256 gadget.
